speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just a bit ago, Paul Harvey on the radio was telling about a woman who just recently was 100 years old. And someone said to her, well, now, to what view mostly? I couldn't think that you were 100 years old. She said to the fact that I was born in 1875. I can't think of a better answer. Well, I wasn't born that soon, quite. But I was born in 1879 on a farm two or three miles from a little town named Van Meter over in Iowa. And when I came to law school, 48 years old, there was a woman from Portland who'd come back to visit in Moscow. She had lived here. I'm sure she'd been over in Portland. She'd come back for a little visit in Portland. And she was one of the Van Meters for whom that town was named, just a little world. Every now and then, I get told on my goodwill work of the name of someone I had known in Harvey, North Dakota, or in Redfield, South Dakota, or in Moore, Montana, or over in Washington, or somewhere, or others. Just a little bit of the world. But anyway, we're here to have a good time together. And just to set the stage for what my life has been, I'll tell you a little incident that happened when I was about three years old. You wouldn't think it now, perhaps, but I was so shy that I would be physically ill if I had to meet a stranger. And one afternoon, Mother and I were and two callers were sitting visiting by the open door. And they kept talking about my gold curls and blue eyes. It's an awful thing for a child to have gold curls and blue eyes. Because people make such a fuss over it. And they don't give you any privacy at all about it. But anyway, I was so frightened of them that I got behind Mother's chair. And that brought me between her and the open door. And after the three of them got busy enough talking that they wouldn't notice me, I slipped out of that open door. And just a little way from that open door, there was the well where we got all the water we used. And the well had a square board curve that came up, I presume, about that high. I don't know. But it couldn't have been very, very high. And it, instead of being set square on the board cover of the well, had been set cornering like this with the two squares. So that inside of this standing up curve, there was a small three-corner piece of the board of the covering over the well. Well, I wanted a place to hide. And it looked to me like a good chance. So I went over to the well. And I can remember now, I got hold of the top of that curve and how I heaved on my chunky little body to get it up over at the top of that. But I did. And I dropped down on this little three-corner piece board right here just above the water. And there I crouched. And after a while, I heard Mother say, I wonder where Clara is. I must see. Well, the three of them went out. And Mother called my name. And immediately, the other two would call my name. When Mother would call my name, I'd start to rise up and climb out. And when the two strangers would call my name, I'd crouch right down there again, just above the water. And by and by, Mother said, well, I have to look in the well. And I could not understand how it was that she'd rubbed both of my arms so hard that it really hurt. Mother, holding my arms so hard, it hurt. I just couldn't think it to be true, but it was. Well, I can understand it later why. Well, that was then. And then there was the time of the, oh, no, I'm not going to tell you that incident now. I'm going to tell you something else. I've had quite a varied life. I guess I've had about everything, among other little things. When I was 82 years of age, I went up to the university to enroll as a student. Well, the reason I was doing it was that my daughter had been talking. She and her husband both graduated here in 31. She had been talking about me going to university, which I'd never had the opportunity of doing. So this time, when she was home for her summer visit, she said, Mother, you go up on that hill and enroll. Well, she had been a student and graduated here, but she didn't stop to think that enrollment was over for this year. So as soon as she got on her bus, I went up on the hill and said, I wanted to enroll. You can't. Well, I said, that was what I came for. You can't. Enrollment has closed for the year. I said, well, anyway, I want to enroll. And she said, well, you'll go and see Dean. Anyway, you'll go and see somebody. Names will not stay with me at all. But anyway, I went to see him, and he was just leaving, and not only leaving, but leaving town for a couple of days. I don't know whether it's because I was going to enroll or what. I don't know. But anyway, he sent me to Dean. You'd all know the name in a minute if I could think of it. But anyway, I went to him and said, I had come to enroll. Well, he said, you can't. Would you like a ride home? I said, no, thank you. I plan to get lunch on campus and enroll and go to class this afternoon. Now, if you want to know who the greenest green frosh they ever had was, you're meeting him. But anyway, he saw that he couldn't drive me home. It was noontime. So he said, well, we'll come back at 1 o'clock. So I went back there before 1. And he talked to me a while about it. And he had a protégé who was under his wing, who was teaching, of course. And he talked with me a while. And he asked this protégé of his if he would take me in his class. Well, a fellow of very good nature just said, yes, he would. I went to class at 1 o'clock that afternoon. And I went right on for two years. And I planned definitely to go a third year or possibly a fourth. But oh, no, I was stricken down the bed for too long a time to think about ever going back. And although I wasn't in the bed for 10 years, then I would be sort of hung around for 10 years. And by that time, I knew that I was not capable of doing the class work. You probably all know the name Ray Gibbs. And for my last semester, I was determined to get into Ray Gibbs' journalism class. I understood perfectly well why Ray Gibbs didn't want me. There had once been a returned missionary on my campus. And she enrolled in everything clear down the alphabet and attended every class and took the whole class to herself. Well, Ray Gibbs was afraid to have an old lady come in and take the class for fear the students wouldn't get enough out of it. Well, for one thing, I knew what he was afraid of. I used to teach myself. I had seven years of it before I married. And I didn't say married at that time. I said, took a school of war, and that's the way you'll announce your marriage. But anyway, I was determined to get into Ray Gibbs' class. And he and this dean talked together quite a while trying to say what they wanted to without me understanding what they were saying. But I had a pretty good idea of it anyway. And finally, he said, yes, I might get into his class. There was one time the whole semester that I spoke when I was not spoken to. And that was the next to last class. I must tell you how Ray Gibbs introduced himself to the class. He stood up before us very reluctantly, sort of. And he said, I am not a professor. I am Ray Gibbs. And the first one in this class to sell a manuscript may have the privilege of, and here we sat just like this. We were going to have the privilege of buying coffee for the class. Well, the next to last class, as Mr. Gibbs started to rise from his chair after dismissing us, I got up quick. And I handed the letter to Mr. Gibbs. And I said, Mr. Gibbs, would you please read this? He looked at me in astonishment. Now, this was the one time that I spoke when I hadn't been spoken to. And he looked at me a little bit. And he said, why, this is a manuscript acceptance. I was the only one in the class who did sell a manuscript that year. And I turned around to the class. And I said, would anybody like a cup of coffee? And Mr. Gibbs said, oh, Mrs. Gold, you don't have to do that. I said, Mr. Gibbs, I worked a whole semester for it. Are you going to cheat me out of it? He said, no, I'm not. Well, now, there was this little shot right here. To you students, the Student Union is just a place. And you know all of it. You've been everywhere in it. All familiar to you. And all I had ever been in the Student Union was in the lower hall and in the office. That's all I knew about the Student Union. So I insisted that I buy coffee for the class. And Mr. Gibbs said, all right. He said, the next class is our best class of the year. And we'll meet at the Student Union at the usual time. And Mrs. Gold would buy the coffee, which I very happily did. And we went up in the room with the stars ceiling. You know it, I'm sure. Anyway, maybe it's probably been torn out now. There was an upper place where the ceiling was stars and moons and so on. And it was really interesting to me to be there. I'd never seen it before. And we had our coffee. And when we finished it, he said, now put your chairs up close. So they shoved the second table up and pulled their chairs up. And he told us, and Rick Gibbs writes in the most interesting way. And he speaks in the same way that he writes. I was extremely interested in what he said. And the rest of them were bored almost to tears before they got through. I didn't care. I was having a good time. But he was telling us about a manuscript he had written and sent to one of the figures of the United States magazines. And it came back. And he said he felt so terrible about it that he just threw it in his desk and thought no more about it for a couple of weeks. And then he thought, well, I want just as well open it and see. So he opened it. And here was a letter. Dear Mr. Gibbs, this manuscript is exactly what we want, except that we want it in depth. And we want you to take your family and at our expense retrace every step of your trip on which you wrote this manuscript and rewrite it for us. So that was what he did. He left his family somewhere in the east for people. He went on to New York. And he told us how he went to the top of the Times Square to the office of this magazine. And the second in command said that the head man would be back in one hour. And that he thought, with his glance at the manuscript, that it was what they would want. But it lay entirely with the head. And for him just to come back in one hour, and he would get his answer. Well, he said he went down to the ground floor. And he walked around and around and around Times Square. And every time around, he looked at his watch, because the hour must be up now. But it wasn't. But when the hour was up, he went back and they accepted his manuscript. Well, I don't know what he got for it. It might have been $2,000 or $3,000, something like that. Anyway, it would have been real money. That was one thing that I did. And I have done so many more things. I'm not going to tell you any more of them now. My name is Clara Marcella Grove. And the Marcella was given me by my mother, because it was a given name of a schoolteacher who was very special to my mother. So I never write my name without this initial in memory of my mother, of which Clara am. Now, I want the rest of you just to start writing in and say whatever you want to or ask whatever you want to, only let's don't have any blank pauses. There's no need of them when they're not comfortable. Who's first? Anybody.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, when we were driving to campus, you said that the campus had changed an awful lot since you first had seen it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: My hearing is pitiful. OK. May I say, the way to speak to any person whose hearing is difficult, look directly at the person. And instead of trying to speak so loud, speak clearly and a little bit slowly, because it is not all in the hearing. It is partly because all of the reflexes are slowed down. Not so much in some people, but quite a lot in other people. And the reflex of being slowed down, we hear the voice, but we don't understand the words. So if they are spoken clearly with the mouth wide open when you speak to them, and a little bit slowly, the person is much more likely to get the whole import of it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How has the campus changed?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, how has the campus changed? Well, the things that are still familiar to me is Morrow Hall and the Science Building and the Ad. And the rest of it is just a great huge big hodgepodge that's thrown about everywhere. That's how I was here. So there was, in that row of dwelling houses, I don't know whether any of them are there yet or not. I haven't been on the campus for a year or two. Two years, I guess it is. But there was what had been a dwelling house that was farmhouse. And then later they moved over and had a real farmhouse. But the Student Union wasn't anything like it has been for years now. It was just there. Just a good sized building and quite ambitious for that time and for what else was on the campus. The ATO, are they still in the same location? I cooked for six years in the Alpha Chi Omega, but that's been moved. I was with the Tri-Delts for a year. I presume they're still there. And across from them is the same.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yellow Delta is not the same.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But there's still some of the old landmarks. But the Engineering Building was just a little bit to the right and in front of the Anne. It was a little bigger than this house, but not so awfully much. And that was the Engineering Building that put my son-in-law through. There are some of the other buildings, but the Teaks were right across from where the Alpha Chi was. I don't know. They're not there now. They have a real ambitious building. They were there. And I'm trying to think of two of them next to each other on my other side of Deacon, pretty well down this way. Anyway, I think they're still there. But all told, it is so different that I think if I tried to come up here myself, I could get so lost the police couldn't find me. But who else wants to know something?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What courses did you take?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was taking a journalism course. I wish I could remember the name of the good man who did get me in. The trouble was, they couldn't have me just sitting on the campus forever. And I wouldn't leave. Why would they want to take me? Well, when they enrolled me, then I went home with the proper intervals. Otherwise, I wasn't going.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was a good kid.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But as for Rick Gibbs, there never was a better teacher than Rick Gibbs. Nobody ever stole his class from him. And he made one mistake in a whole semester. And he said there, I shouldn't have said that. I should have waited for you to say it. That's the only mistake that he made that whole semester. He was in absolute control of that class. He said that with only one manuscript accepted, that he blamed himself. Well, I don't think he was to blame. I think he gave us all that anybody could give from a teacher's desk. And I did enjoy that semester so much. What was it you wanted to know?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When you first came to Moscow, what did you do?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I worked for a little while in the newspaper office for, I was going to tell you his name, and it slipped away from me, the man who was there then. He died years ago. I was there a little while. But most of the time I've been in Moscow, I've been either cooking or nursing. I've nursed at the Moscow Hospital and in the clinic in Colfax and the sister's hospital in Colfax, all three of them. And I did private nursing mostly for quite a long time. I like the nursing work very much. And I cooked one year in Poland, my first year, just part of the year. I cooked what they had. Unfortunately, I just couldn't manage the cooking. So I replaced her during not so far into the term. And I cooked for the Avokai Omega there. And since that, they abandoned the dwelling in which they were housed and built farther up on the campus. They had just a dwelling, a two-story dwelling. And the cook had a shanty out in the backyard. I lived out there while I cooked for the Avokai Omega in Poland. But it was nice and quiet out there. And I had the compliment when I left. One of the girls said, I wish you wouldn't leave. I like your cooking. Well, that makes you feel good no matter what you're doing, if somebody likes what you did. Was something right there that you wanted to say? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You said that you taught for six or seven years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you teach for six or seven years?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Teaching? Did you teach?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I taught for seven years. I taught country schools, except in one year, I taught the first three grades in Darneil, Montana, town. That is, we called it the town. We had a general store with a post office in it. And we had a home right across the street from it. And there was a hotel with, I think, four rooms. Might have been five, possibly. Not any more, I'm sure. And we had a schoolhouse over here. And then over here was my schoolhouse, an early day cabin that somebody had built and gone away leaving it there. And they used it for the first three grades. I wasn't quite as old then as I am now. I was kind of young and green about some things. And one morning, we had a guest at school, a very important guest, I thought. And it was quite customary in the schools at that time that we had some kind of an opening exercise every morning. I think all schools had something. And it was very customary that they recited quotations, such as, "'Tis hard and glorious to be poor, and empty sack, but hard to stand upright, but if it does, just stomp on it." All that kind of thing. Well, I was going to show off before this teacher. And I said, we'll have quotations this morning. And we started right here. And by the way, one of those boys with his mother had a store over in Pullman for years. But anyway, here one boy stands up, and there had been a little road show. I don't know whether you know what a road show is or not. I can tell you if you want to know. A little road show had been in the town the night before. And these two little boys had attended the road show. And one of these little boys upped up from his seat, and he said, "'Turkey in the straw, ha, ha, ha.'" Well, my hair was standing right on the end. But the other little boy pops up, and he says, "'Turkey in the hay, hay, hay, hay.'" I thought I was ruined before I did. Do you know what a road show is? No. Like a medicine show? Well, they had one in Troy when I lived there, which I did two years before I came here 48 years ago. And dad and mother and the upper teenage son and daughter were the road show. And dad didn't have to say, "'I hate this, and I told them not to do it, and I won't do it.'" It had been written all over him. He didn't need to say it. But anyway, I went to the little road show. And when it came dad's turn to speak, he just stands there, and the son repeats his lines for him. And dad won't say them. I didn't blame dad any. Their dialogue, well, it wasn't anything. It was just a little collection of words back and forth, but there was nothing to it. Nothing funny, nothing interesting, nothing entertaining. Just a little back and forth talk, and dad wouldn't take his part. But that's a road show, when people just get up something that they can. And in those days, of course, they went about with the horse and wagon. Of course, now they have a car. And there are enough other shows that a road show, well, it's unique. It might have quite a big patronage, because it wouldn't be different. Was there something you wanted to ask me? Mrs. Groh, how do you keep going when you get discouraged sometimes? I will have to go way back to the time my daughter and her husband lived in Denver, Colorado. And I visited her every summer for 13 summers. And she always took me to see her doctor. He was one of the most unusual doctors that I have ever met, and I've met a lot of them. And he knew more about my physical and mental condition than any other doctor that I ever saw. And as I saw him for the last time, he said, Now, Mrs. Groh, just keep going. Are the only comfortable, reasonable, pleasant years that I've had. Well, I wanted to eat the next meal every time, and if I did, I had to keep going. So I did keep going, and the background of this man, this good doctor, telling me this, has had a large play in the fact. Just, it's really real personal, you'll pardon me, I know. But just two or three weeks ago, I had a whole entire week, Sunday to Sunday, that I called the recession. Well, right after it, I had what I called a Renaissance. Well, during this thing I called the recession, You know, you might be 96 someday, you might tell me. I hope I will. My point is, I wasn't ill in any way, whatever. I wasn't suffering at all. I just wasn't there. I would just lie on my bed, the usual hours. I would get up and sit in my chair, and there I would sit. I wasn't there. It was a real recession. And I could not summon an ambition to go on. I think the reason was that I had been terribly physically overworking. And I think I had used up all the physical resource to push the mental. But suddenly, it's over. And as for health, I have better health these late years than I ever had. Well, I've been alone 44 of these 48 years. We came from Troy. And by the way, my daughter and I owned the Troy News at one time. And Wilbert Johns, from whom I bought it, or who sold it to me, is that a way to state it? I had known him in Montana. He had the paper there. And I had been reporter for him. And I had dabbled on that reporting career for 19 years. And one day, he and I, to make a claim to you, we hand-set the type. We didn't use a machine. We just picked up one letter after another and put it in that box. And then we took it to the stone and emptied that when we had it full, went back and filled it up again. Well, it happened that Mr. Johns and myself were both setting types in two different cases. And we both got the stone at the same time. And as we were emptying our type onto the stone, all at once he lifted his head and looked at me and he said, Mrs. Grove, do you want to buy this paper? And I said, yes, I do. Just like that. He said, well, then let's go to the bank and make out the papers. And I said, well, let's go. And then 15 minutes from the time I ever had heard about that he was going to sell it or I was going to buy it, I owned it, and the press. Now, don't miss the press on that. The press was a huge old thing. Well, it took nearly like a quarter of this room. It was a huge thing. And in order to feed it, it hand-fed, of course. I stood on a box about this tall and reached up here and fed the papers in. And the first few I fed in, I thought every other one or every third or fourth one would wind around the roller instead of going on onto the platform. I had never run a press. I knew nothing about it. I had been setting type, learned from Mr. Johns, and doing a little general work. But there were things I knew nothing about. But anyway, I owned it. I presume you don't know what boilerplate is. Anyway, it's a type that has been set up and then molded into a solid block on a base. And a newspaper keeps more or less of that on hand in case they have to go to press and there's a blank spot. They get this boilerplate and print that in there. And it may be something about Queen Victoria or anything else. But anyway, it fills the space so you don't have a blank space on your paper. Anyway, he said, now here's some boilerplate. He said, undoubtedly you're going to need it. Need it? I hadn't been running that paper more than about six weeks until I had to run a supplement to put all the news on. And I had to keep on running a supplement in order to get all the news. But my daughter Ethel was, graduated in Troy. I was ready for university. And the way she came to go to the university, the first time I ever held her in my arms, I began talking to her about when you're big enough, you're going to university. My people were not university people mostly. And I made up my mind that that part of my people were going to the university. And I took that tour until we didn't know anything else but that she was going to university. And one woman said to me one time when we were in real hardship, eating too many, she said, now Mrs. Crowell, you cannot put that child through university. You just send her to business school and in six months she can get a job as secretary and you're all set. Well, Ethel refused always to be a secretary. And I don't believe in forcing a child into something they don't want to work at if it's possible to avoid it. And we had talked this university until maybe we couldn't do it, but we didn't know we couldn't, so we did it. And she got through. And she always boasted to her husband Lawrence like, ha ha, Lawrence, I graduated before you did. She did. She was BA and he was engineering and she went across the platform before he did. She graduated that much before. And they've had quite an adventurous life. They were in Denver, Billings, Montana, Denver, Guam, Tennessee, Washington. And by that time, about 40 years was up and Lawrence retires. And the two of them together built a sumptuous new home right near the Mojave Desert. There's an interesting political fact in connection with them buying land in Lake Mount Zuma near the Mojave Desert. Before Lawrence was an engineer. This is politics, but anyway, everybody ought to know the facts about some politics. Lawrence, before he was an engineer, was a cabinet maker and a carpenter. I always said he was born with a square in one hand and a saw in the other. And that was his natural work, same as engineering is, electrical engineering. So he was determined that he would build his house and he would wear it and he would have it like he wanted it. Well, for the money they had allocated for purchase of land, they could get more land at Lake Mount Zuma than they could in any other place they could find. But beyond that, there was the political fact that unless Lawrence would join a carpenter's union, he could not build his own house. I think that's getting very, very rank. And it's time that everybody got into politics and cleaned them up a little bit. But anyway, they built their house there and there they live in the desert wind and heat, 110°F, a very common summer. Pardon me. I don't know what else these people want to talk about.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Speaking of politics, what's been your favorite president?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We haven't had any favorites in a long period of years. But going way back, by the way, I didn't get hold of my list of the presidents. As I mentioned to you, names do not stay with me. But further back, there were some of the presidents. One of them was Teddy Roosevelt. He was a favorite. Of course, I read all about his doings at the time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Thank you, Cooper.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It probably would interest you to know that I talked with the man who was in the boat with MacArthur when they outran the other parties. Well, I talked with him. And I asked him what he thought of MacArthur. He said, as a soldier, I would follow him into hell, but I have no use for him as a man. And he said, we just got into the boat. Mount Brandon was the only way we got away. And he said, after we were all in the boat, MacArthur sent one of the men back to quarters to get a bottle of wine. And he said, when the enemy got to the bottom of the water, he would be in the water. And he said, would the enemy ride on his heels? No wonder he wouldn't take much of it in the matter. And I don't know why I ever became a villain, MacArthur. We heard so much about him just for a little while, and then never another word. And one of the things we heard at the time was that he had never seen a football game until they were settled here. Someone took him to a football game. My opinion is that maybe he didn't miss much Nazi football. But basketball was my game. You liked basketball? Basketball. And my daughter and I were at a basketball game in New Jersey. It was new at that time. And I don't know why they didn't make a proper egress. You could get in, but when a crowd tried to get out, that was something different. And I was caught in that crowd. And I could just about squeak, and I said, oh! And she just simply, she's bigger and taller, she just simply doubled her arms, get back! And they got back. But I really was being crushed. And before that, there was a time that I was in a crowd, and the police broke up the crush. Who was that president that they said committed suicide on the Alaskan waters? Well, anyway, there was a president who died suddenly. And it was, he did commit suicide because of something that was about to break out in Washington. And some said, no, it wasn't suicide, that he did not suicide, that he was fed food that had stood until it contained a poison element, that it was spoiled. And that was why he died. But that is quite an improbable story, I think. But anyway, I was caught in the... Would you like to have a drink? No, for you.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, thank you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was caught in the line that was waiting to get into the hall where they're having a memorial service for this man. Just a line of this. And they were jammed, so a policeman with his club, he didn't hit anybody, but he threatened with it. And people began to move back a little, but I was caught in that quite unpleasantly. So there is such a thing as being utterly crushed in a crowd. Thank you, it's good.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Thank you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When I enrolled, I presume they have practically the same form for you to fill out that they did then, perhaps so. A form in which you tell all about your beliefs and unbeliefs and what you've done and what you haven't done and so on. And it asks, what occupations have you followed? Well, I started right in the blank that was given there. And I went down with almost face the water below it, and I went up the side, and I went across the top, and I went down here. And I think I had nearly all of them. You folks don't know what hard times are. I've been through them other times, other places, long ago. I was through them in South Dakota. I'm not sure whether, yes, it was South Dakota. It had been Dakota Territory for the first years we lived there. And then it was divided and made into North and South Dakota, and the spelling was changed from D-A-C-O-T-A-H to D-A-K-O-T-A. But we had hard times there. Businessmen who had nothing and no place to go were on the road stopping at doors and asking if they could have some food. I remember Mother Petey. She fed everybody who came along. Not that we had it to spare, but she always had something for them. And we had something always. Someone said to me, just a child, Yes, and someday your mother will find that that man that she's feeding will kill her. Well, the child, of course, I ran home and told Mother. And I've always remembered what Mother said. No man is as dangerous as a hungry man. Would you agree with that? I would. I remember a young couple. There was a time here in Moscow that there was no housing. They hadn't even begun to bring in the abandoned dorms from the Army settlement. They hadn't begun to bring those yet. There was no housing, no such thing. I took in a student couple. And then I took in another student couple. And June said to me one day, Did you hear me and Al fighting? I said, No, I didn't hear anything. Well, she said, We had a fight and it was a serious one. I think they'd been married at least two or three months, maybe a little bit more. Nothing wrong except she didn't know enough to cook and Al was hungry. Now you girls put that up and remember it. And when you get ready to announce your marriage, you just tell them that you've taken the school of one. There you are. What do you think of the women's movement? I think they are silly. One asked me, Wouldn't you like to be equal with men? Now I don't mean any slur at all. I meant the joke. And I said, No, I'm not going to be lowered with the men. I want to stay where I am. If you notice the newspaper pictures of the weddings, if you want to know which is the bride, you have to look and see who wears the veil. Well, now you just notice. The men look like women and the women look like men. It's true among the people you meet to go deal. I don't know what's the matter with you folks here. It doesn't prevail. You're out of date. But it is quite prevalent. Especially in the grade school age. Someone even consulted dear Abby about how could she make it right with the boy that she said was a girl. Do you all read Dear Abby? I do. I always say there wasn't any use for them to publish if they didn't have Dear Abby. But some of the questions I asked are so silly. For instance, there was a woman who said that she needed her back porch so badly and her husband had done a little work on it. And he was so busy helping the neighbor women that he couldn't finish her porch. And what could she do about it? Well, the answer is simple. Call in two or three couples for an evening visit. Put them in a little silence. Just say, well, I'm hoping that my husband will get my back porch finished. I need it. And she's talking loud so everybody hears her. I hope my husband will get my back porch finished soon because I need it so badly. But he's so busy helping the rest of you he can't help me. About the next day that porch would have been finished. You don't have to always hit a person in the face to tell them what you want to say. But I do think some of the questions she gets are very foolish. One boy had one the other day that was quite a pleasure. If anybody knows the answer, do tell Dear Abby about it. He didn't like any of the games, football and so on. And he didn't, well he was a bookie boy. He liked his books and he didn't like those things. Although he said he did like swimming. And he took calisthenics enough to keep himself in fit. Well that's good too. But it doesn't have quite the benefit that a game against the other fellow has. You learn more if you're playing a game against somebody else. You learn a lot more if you do read a book about it. And what could he do because he would go into the eighth grade and he would have to take part in the football and so on. And how could he get out of it? Well I don't know whether you read it or not, but Dear Abby didn't quite know how he could get out of it. That since life is made up of having to take some things like they are, he better just be resigned about it and take it. Which I thought was a very sensible answer. Now what else do you want to talk about?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How many years were you married Mrs. Grove? How many years were you married? How many years were you married?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was married in 1907 and from then on for a while. Mine was not a long marriage. My husband died years ago. So I didn't have a long marriage.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Was it a happy marriage while it lasted? Was it happy?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, it was not a happy marriage. Well I don't think it will go into it. I think we better let it rest right there. Alright. But there are rules for happiness and unhappiness. And one of the great rules for happiness in or out of marriage, anywhere, in the schoolroom, on the street, anywhere you are, is tact. T-A-C-T. And how many, think now for a minute, how many really tactful people do you know? They're scarce. And they're getting scarcer I think. Well this is a different time. Times are not now like they used to be. For instance, in the good old days, a child who would address a grown person by his Christian name instead of saying Mr. Smith would be most certainly reprimanded for it. It was not done. Only relatives and very intimate friends called you by your Christian name. You were Mrs. You were Mr. There really was a depth under that. There was a formality at that time that we don't have now. And that formality was sort of a fence between you and various undesirable traits and performances. It is true that formality is a restraint. Do we have any formality now? I belong to a group of women in which, well the youngest one I would imagine would be middle-aged or close to it. And some of them are old women mostly. I'm not old. I'm only 96. So that isn't old. It was decreed that we were to call each other by our first names. Well when I was a child, you never heard of the women meeting together and calling each other. Calling each other by their first names. It was all Mrs., Mrs., Mrs., Miss. And it is a restraint. It is a good thing. But there is the fact that we don't have it now. We have to get along without it until... You see the trouble is that when people make a change, they don't make a gradual change. They go overboard. Lock, stock and barrel. Right overboard. Let's have something different. Let's destroy that. Let's have something. Anything is different. And that's the way that we go from one era to another. And it's a little bit confusing to some of us who live through a couple of periods. But these years of mine now are the only comfortable years that I've had. I had to live with my grandparents for quite a little while. My grandfather was born in 1812. I had my grandmother in 1824. Oh, I'm going to tell you something. Grandmother always said that she was married when she was 19. Well, that went on. The grandmother had been married in 19 until they'd been married about 50 years. The school teacher one day heard grandmother telling somebody that she was married when she was 19. And I said, my mother, that doesn't work out. You were 19 and you were born in 1824 and you were married in 1845. You math students. Well, to me the funny part of it was grandmother considered that a child lost his mother. There was a little quibble. But she was determined. Everything had to be exactly as she did it because her mother had done it that way. And certainly her mother did it right. And she did it like her mother did. So why did we want to do it any differently? Well, being right about the work, Uncle Will and myself got up at 5 in the morning. Grandmother had probably been up and in the garden for an hour before that. But by 9 o'clock or 10 at the latest, my grandmother came in and laid down on her bed. And she slept for one to two hours. And in the afternoon she went back to her garden for a little bit just to be sure it was all there and it loved her and all that kind of thing. And then she lay down on her bed and slept for one or two hours and went to bed at 8 o'clock. And Uncle Will came in for his supper. Now I had supper for my grandfather and grandmother when it sprayed up 6 o'clock. They came to the table. And Uncle Will came in sometime between 8 and 9, usually about 9, with a pail of milk. And I gave him his hot supper that I had cooked for him and took care of the milk. And then I was free to go to bed about 10 and stay until 5. And the only salvation that there was for me, possibly, there was no other, was that I keep at work from the time I got up at 5 o'clock until I went to bed at 10 o'clock. Why you were a desperado if you didn't work all of the time. There was something wrong with your head. Why wouldn't you be at work? Well, that's the way it was there. And she spoke kindly to me once while I was there. I've always remembered that. And I knew that Grandfather told her she had to. And we were getting, she and I were getting the eggs and the butter ready for Uncle Will to take to town. And she amazed me by speaking nicely and saying, No, I was going to take him to town, not Uncle Will, I was going to take him. She amazed me by saying, Now you get a quarter's worth of sugar and a pound of coffee and you can have what else the eggs bring for yourself. I nearly fell over with surprise. And those South Dakota plains were some place to live. The annual rainfall was 14 inches. There were people trying to raise crops. I remember the night that Uncle Will did his thrashing. He did his full thrashing one day at that time with a binder. They cut the grain, bound into bundles, and then a man followed and set these up, four bundles in a bunch, leading against each other so they stood up. And then the thrashers came and two men on a wagon with pitchforks threw these into the wagon and hauled them to the machine, the thrashing machine, and they were thrashed. It was all that operation to get the separation of the wheat and the straw. Uncle Will came in after the thrashers had finished and gone. It was just about 9 o'clock when he came in. I saw right away that I was giving supper to a sick man. So I waited until he'd nearly finished his supper and I said, How many bushels did you have, Will? He had 100 acres and he had 300 bushels. And that same year there was a woman who had planted as a sort of garden predator 5 acres of squall corn. I'm sure you've never seen squall corn. It grows about so high and it puts out two or three ears on one stalk. And it's really a field corn. And oh how we loved that corn. It was all the corn we had from green corn. And it wasn't quite as fieldy as the real field corn. But this woman had over her 5 acres of squall corn and got enough for the thrasher men's supper. I'll tell you those were lean times. And there was a man at Mallette. Hawthorne was our town. Mallette was probably 60 or 80 miles from there. There was an article in the paper that so-and-so at Mallette had harvested 12 bushels to the acre of his wheat. And I read the article to Grandfather. He said, oh yes, Uncle Duke, I'll give you a paper story. But anybody knows that he never did it. 12 bushels. Nobody ever did that. Well, it was the first man anywhere around there that had gotten 12 bushels to the acre. And he had used that brand new dust mulch idea. I just thought of a thing. And that was in the late 1800s. But he had really raised 12 bushels to the acre. And I kept hearing from people there, friends, relatives, about there being so much rain that they were just raved out. And I said, well, if I could see it, I could believe it. Well, I went through that same territory, not through Falkland, but through Aberdeen and Redfield and Curran. And I saw a cornfield that had been planted in a railroad ditch. And they would build the track up from the level of the ground about a foot and a half, something like that. They would build it up, build the track on this elevation. And then there would be this ditch on each side that would be perhaps a way. And then I saw a place where that was planted to corn. And in mid-July, that corn was standing in three or four inches of water. Well, I had to believe that South Dakota had gotten too wet. Who knows what gumbo is? You know. Tell us. It's hard clay that nothing will soak through. Just stay there. It's just about as near, well, like plastic as it could be, and still be soil. But these ditches would hold water. We hauled water in barrels to haveage. It was a common thing. You'd put a barrel on a stone boat, or maybe two barrels on a stone boat, and hitch a horse to it and haul water from where you could get it. And sometimes there was a long way to it. The gumbo would hold the water longer than any other soil would. And there was one family that was having no water at that time, excepting what she got in this railroad ditch. That's all the water supply they had. And she was washing one day when a neighbor woman came in. And she said, well, how do you get your clothes to look like anything washing them in that water? Oh, she said, they may be the whiter, but they may smell the sweeter. So she wasn't letting herself worry because she had no decent water. And at my grandfather's, you can see how Hoosiers, who believed in working from daylight till dark without a minute of do-things, they had built their house up here. And when you went over here about a quarter of a mile, and down into the coulee, there was a spring that never ran dry. It ran all year. And we got our water from there in a barrel, hitched a horse to the stone boat. And she called it in that way. And that was the water that we had. And it was very good water in that spring. Well, by and by, grandmother suddenly died. And my sister gave up her school and went to keep house for her grandfather in Oakland, Wales. And she was not for work like grandmother was, but she was for having her own way like grandmother was. And she wanted then to dig a well up here by the house. No, no use. No use to do it. There's no water there. Well, right here by the house, it was dry gravel. But over here, just a matter of less than a hundred feet, maybe fifty feet, there was a little sort of depression. And over here, there was nothing on and on and on but the buffalo grass. And over here in this little depression, the grass grew green and about that tall. Well, she just had an idea there must be something to make that difference. And she remembered that right down here in the coulee was that spring that never ran dry. So she wanted a well. Nope, no use. She knew how to get it. She said, well, don't dig the well and I won't stay. I'll leave. They dug that well. And I never could remember whether it was forty or sixty feet. Sixty wasn't considered a deep well. A hundred was deep. But they dug a well and they got a supply that they could not pump dry, ever. And there for forty, fifty years, no it wasn't fifty but for many years, they had lived right here hauling water in a barrel. I don't know what they did without that exercise. Laughter I'll tell you a life on the plains in those times was something. I know one time I was four when we went from Iowa to Dakota Territory. And I had a brother who was ten years older than I was. Well, the difference between four and fourteen is quite a lot. It isn't so much between some other ages but right there it's a big number. One day I was saying something about grandfather and grandmother being so awfully harsh and so harsh with all the children and grandchildren. And this oldest brother of mine said, well, they tamed the continent. They did. And I had great times doing it. And the first recollection we had of our family, by the way, when I bought our place here, our home over on the other side of town, I named it Blarney Castle. And when I bought it, it consisted of two rooms only. Nothing more. I'm out in front of those alfalfa that was more than knee high. Most beautiful alfalfa crop I ever saw. Went from the house here to the street. I've got most of it out. I have a little of it left but I don't try to get out. But anyway, I named it Blarney Castle. And when we had first registered at the university and giving the Methodist church as our preference, the Methodist minister, of course, came to call. And I welcomed him to Blarney Castle. And after a little he said, well, why do you call this Blarney Castle? I said, well, don't you think it would take a lot of Blarney to make you think it is a castle? And beyond that, the earliest, one of the earliest ancestors that I know anything about had kissed the Blarney stone. So if anyone asks me my nationality, I don't admit to English or the Swiss Dutch at all. I'm Irish. This ancestor of mine, when he was a housekeeping teenage boy, went from his inland home in Ireland to the coast to see the ships. And he was walking along back and forth on the dock so delighted that he could see the ocean and the ships. And the sailor came up to him and he said, boy, would you like to see the inside of the ship? And what teenage boy wouldn't like to? So they went down and the sailor showed him everything on deck and explained it all. And he said, let's go down now and see what's below. So they went down to see what was below. And the boy said, what's in this room? And the sailor took the bar off the door and he said, well, go in and see. The boy got to see. When he was in, they both were shocked again with the sailor on the outside. And he was kept in there until they were so far at sea that there would be no possibility of him leaving. And then he was put on deck with the others, put to work with the others. And when they reached this shore, there were no harbors, no wharfs. There were harbors but no wharfs. But they anchored far enough in the harbor that they thought nobody could possibly swim to shore. And the crew, because it was hot weather all the way across the Atlantic, had slept on the deck. When they were sleeping, they just lay on the deck and slept. That's all there was to it. They had pretty rough times for sailors at that time. And he with the other sailors were there. When they anchored far enough, they thought no one could swim. But he had Irish blood. And he just didn't want to be indentured. Do you all know what indentured is? Of course you do. That's when he would be sold to some farmer and would have to work as a slave until he was 21. And when he would be 21, it was supposed that the owner would give him a horse, bridle, and saddle. Sometimes the owner did. But he was free at 21. And if he tried to leave before he was 21, he was fair game for anybody's bullet. It wasn't murder. It was proper punishment for leaving before he would be 21. So there weren't many that tried to leave because there was no place to go. Well, this fine young Irish lad in his teens didn't want to be indentured. So during the night, he managed to slip overboard without being heard. And he swam to shore. And the minute he was on shore, he started running. Well, he hadn't even heard much about this country. He knew there was a country here, and that's about all. But he started running with no destination except to get away from the water. Get far enough from the water that he couldn't be overtaken. And he did. Well, now that is the most that I know about him, practically all that I know about him. But that is the Irish line that we have and how we got it. And my grandfather was a fine old Irish gentleman. And at that time, there were very few really tall people. And he was 6'3". And held himself very erect. And when he was 75, his children said to him, Now, father, we have tried for years to get you to quit working on the farm. You're too old. Just 75. And you just have to quit now. This is your 75th birthday, and you are not going out to the field today. You're not going to the field again. He sat down in his chair and sat there until he was 92. The extent of his activities during all those years was that he sometimes emptied the ash for grandmother. And he practically always did the churning for grandmother. And you churned like this. And he could bring the butter past to the many butt fields that ever were churned. And he just very calmly went at it just like that, and there's the butter.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mrs. Grove, I think we should probably stop.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think we should. I think we should, and I'll be just so glad to meet all of you again. We're going to have good times together, and you should be primed up with what you want to ask and what you want to tell. Anyone of you knows something interesting that might be useful, if known. Because sometimes some of the most useful things have come out of some little incident that seemed to have no point to it. So thanking you all.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When would you, how soon, or when would you like to get together again?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I think that perhaps you and the class should decide it. My time is not taken like other people's time. Of course, I do have my good will. I am the master manager of the good will, and have been for ten years. A most interesting position. I meet such interesting people, both on the phone and in person. So I think you and the others should decide.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How would five o'clock be on Thursday, rather than four o'clock? You just sit like this, do you? Sorry. Two weeks.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Two weeks. Is that alright with everybody? Great.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Two weeks, same time, same place. We'll meet again in two weeks.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Two weeks.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Same time. And I'll come and get you again. I'll take you home now. I'll have better luck now. I know where you are.
